item.title: Judge labels police assault ‘bullying’, jails officer
item.description: High Court judge has described the actions of a police officer who seriously injured a man in custody as a case of “Police bullying”, saying the abuse of authority undermined public confidence in the Fiji Police Force. Justice Thusara Rajasinghe made the comments while sentencing Apimeliki Vakarusabola Colamoto yesterday to three years imprisonment for one count of act with intent to cause grievou
item.content:encoded:
High Court judge has described the actions of a police officer who seriously injured a man in custody as a case of “Police bullying”, saying the abuse of authority undermined public confidence in the Fiji Police Force.

Justice Thusara Rajasinghe made the comments while sentencing Apimeliki Vakarusabola Colamoto yesterday to three years imprisonment for one count of act with intent to cause grievous harm.

Colamoto will serve 18 months immediately, while the remaining 18 months has been suspended for three years. After accounting for nearly nine days already spent in custody, he will serve 17 months and 20 days.

“I term this a case of Police bullying,” Justice Rajasinghe said.

The court heard Colamoto arrested the complainant in Nausori Town after the man questioned why Police had failed to stop a brawl from escalating.

After taking him to the police station, Colamoto punched the complainant in the face when he asked why he had been arrested.

The assault caused a complete fracture of the man’s jawbone, requiring surgery and wires to maintain the integrity of his jaw.

Justice Rajasinghe said the conduct represented a serious abuse of the authority entrusted to a police officer.

“You abused your authority by assaulting the Complainant, who was in your custody at the Police Station; such behaviour is reprehensible,” he said.

The judge said crimes committed by police officers had broader consequences because of the trust placed in them by the public.

“Crimes of this nature involving members of the Police Force undermine the confidence the public is legitimately entitled to place in the Police Force to maintain law and order within the bounds of the laws of the Country,” Justice Rajasinghe said.

He found the seriousness of the offending to be “exceptionally high” and said deterrence was a primary consideration in sentencing.

“A custodial sentence is inevitable for offences of this nature to demonstrate the gravity of the offence and to reflect that society denounces such crimes without any reservation,” he said.

Justice Rajasinghe also treated Colamoto’s breach of the trust placed in him by both the Police Force and the public as an aggravating factor.

Colamoto has 30 days to appeal to the Fiji Court of Appeal.

item.title: Pressure forced Government’s tourism tax reversal – Kumar
item.description: Opposition MP Premila Kumar says pressure from Fiji’s tourism industry forced the Government to change its position on the Tourism Services Tax, describing the decision as a “victory for common sense”. The Government has confirmed that the new five per cent TST will apply only to bookings made on or after September 1, 2026, meaning existing bookings will be exempt even if the service is provided a
item.content:encoded:
Opposition MP Premila Kumar says pressure from Fiji’s tourism industry forced the Government to change its position on the Tourism Services Tax, describing the decision as a “victory for common sense”.

The Government has confirmed that the new five per cent TST will apply only to bookings made on or after September 1, 2026, meaning existing bookings will be exempt even if the service is provided after that date.

Ms Kumar welcomed the decision but questioned why industry pressure was required to secure the change.

“This is the right decision. But why did it take pressure from the tourism industry to get Government to do what should have been agreed during consultation in the first place?” she said.

Ms Kumar said the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association had raised concerns about protecting existing bookings and contractual arrangements, while she had also called for the issue to be reconsidered in Parliament.

“My concerns were ignored at the time,” she said.

She argued the reversal highlighted broader concerns about the Government’s approach to economic policymaking.

“Government cannot first ignore the industry’s concerns and then blame the industry for objecting,” Ms Kumar said.

“The Government’s reversal today demonstrates that the industry’s concerns were legitimate.”

She said tourism generated billions of dollars in foreign exchange and supported thousands of businesses and livelihoods, making it important that policies affecting the sector were developed with careful consideration of their wider impact.

Ms Kumar warned that tourism businesses were already dealing with rising costs, new regulatory requirements and uncertainty surrounding other legislation.

“Fiji cannot afford to make itself a more expensive and less competitive destination,” she said.

She called on the Government to assess the combined impact of taxation and regulation on Fiji’s competitiveness and develop a long-term strategy focused on growing the tourism industry rather than increasing revenue collection from it.

“Decision on tourism services tax is a victory for common sense and for the tourism industry,” Ms Kumar said.

item.title: Kiran calls for return to “veilomani, veirokovi”
item.description: Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran has called on Fijians to strengthen the traditional values of veilomani — love for one another — and veirokovi — respect for one another, amid concerns over recent robberies and burglaries. Ms Kiran said communities had a shared responsibility to protect vulnerable people, particularly older persons and those living alone.
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran has called on Fijians to strengthen the traditional values of veilomani — love for one another — and veirokovi — respect for one another, amid concerns over recent robberies and burglaries.

Ms Kiran said communities had a shared responsibility to protect vulnerable people, particularly older persons and those living alone.

“We must strengthen the values that have always held our communities together — veilomani, love for one another, and veirokovi, respect for one another,” she said.

“Let us know our neighbours, check on our elderly and look out for those who are vulnerable.”

Her comments follow the reported robbery of 80-year-old Mahendra Nath at his home in Rokara Settlement, Khalsa Road.

According to reports, basic groceries including rice, sugar, tinned food, cooking oil and powdered milk were allegedly taken, along with household items, tools, clothing and cash.

Ms Kiran said the incident demonstrated why communities needed to look out for one another.

“When an 80-year-old man has even his basic food supplies taken from him, this goes beyond the loss of property — it takes away his sense of safety, independence and dignity,” she said.

The Minister said Fiji could not allow crimes against vulnerable people to become normalised or simply become incidents watched and discussed on social media before being forgotten.

She also urged parents and guardians to reinforce the importance of honesty, hard work and respect for other people’s belongings among young people.

“Teach our young people to respect the hard-earned income and belongings of others,” Ms Kiran said.

“What may appear to be an easy gain represents someone else’s hours of work, sacrifice and saving.”

Ms Kiran encouraged communities to establish or strengthen Neighbourhood Watch zones, work closely with Police and regularly check on elderly people living alone.

“Protecting one another is a shared responsibility, and we must never allow crime against the vulnerable to become normal,” she said.

item.title: Tourism, remittances keep Fiji economy on positive track
item.description: Fiji’s economy continues to show encouraging signs, with record July visitor arrivals, strong remittance inflows and resilient investment activity supporting the country’s growth outlook, says Reserve Bank of Fiji Governor and Board Chairman Ariff Ali. Mr Ali said visitor arrivals reached 105,791 in July, the highest ever recorded for the month and 6.5 per cent above July 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s economy continues to show encouraging signs, with record July visitor arrivals, strong remittance inflows and resilient investment activity supporting the country’s growth outlook, says Reserve Bank of Fiji Governor and Board Chairman Ariff Ali.

Mr Ali said visitor arrivals reached 105,791 in July, the highest ever recorded for the month and 6.5 per cent above July 2025.

The result lifted cumulative visitor growth to 4.3 per cent for the first seven months of 2026.

“Economic activity remains encouraging,” Mr Ali said in a statement.

He said strong tourism activity, combined with a 26.3 per cent increase in remittance inflows during the first six months of the year, continued to support household consumption.

Investment also remained resilient, supported by increased lending and construction activity.

“Against this backdrop, the outlook for economic growth in 2026 remains positive, with recent indicators suggesting some potential for growth to be stronger than currently anticipated,” Mr Ali said.

Financial conditions remained supportive, with banking system liquidity at around $2 billion as of August 26 and private sector credit growing by 14.6 per cent in July.

However, Mr Ali warned that the economy continued to face significant risks from inflation, election-related uncertainty, social and security concerns, geopolitical tensions and energy market volatility.

Headline inflation stood at 5.7 per cent in July, down slightly from 6.1 per cent in June but substantially higher than the negative 1.5 per cent recorded a year earlier.

Higher fuel, gas and kerosene prices accounted for about 2.8 percentage points of July’s inflation.

Inflation is expected to remain elevated in coming months as higher global fuel prices and freight costs flow through to domestic prices.

Foreign reserves stood at $3.9 billion as of August 27, sufficient to cover 5.5 months of retained imports.

Mr Ali said reserves were being supported by government external loan drawdowns, strong tourism receipts and remittance inflows and were expected to remain adequate over the medium term.

item.title: Police defend operations, claiming serious crime rates have decreased
item.description: The Fiji Police Force says serious crime rates have declined this year despite recent public criticism over aggravated robberies and burglaries, with Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu calling for a nationwide approach to tackling the causes of crime. Mr Tudravu said Police accepted criticism of its operations following several high-profile incidents and was adjusting strategies to ensure respons
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Police Force says serious crime rates have declined this year despite recent public criticism over aggravated robberies and burglaries, with Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu calling for a nationwide approach to tackling the causes of crime.

Mr Tudravu said Police accepted criticism of its operations following several high-profile incidents and was adjusting strategies to ensure responses were proactive rather than reactive.

Police statistics for January to July 2026 show burglary declined by 7.3 per cent, robbery by 32.8 per cent, aggravated robbery by 17.8 per cent, aggravated burglary by 7.7 per cent and theft by 7.9 per cent compared with the same period last year.

However, motor vehicle theft increased from 31 cases during the first seven months of 2025 to 51 this year.

Overall crime declined by 11 per cent, from 11,387 cases in January-July 2025 to 10,106 during the corresponding period this year.

“The posture and strategies adopted by operations for the first six months has resulted in the reduction in these crimes,” Mr Tudravu said.

He acknowledged the figures could be met with scepticism amid recent cases attracting significant public attention.

“While this will be met with scepticism, the Fiji Police Force accepts constructive criticism to avoid predictable policing patterns that may be exploited by offenders,” he said.

Mr Tudravu said arrests alone would not provide a lasting solution and called for greater attention to why people repeatedly committed crimes.

“The why factor. This is where we need to also focus our attention as a nation,” he said.

“We have individuals coming into the system who are habitual offenders with multiple theft or burglary cases, which begs two critical questions, why and what can be an effective deterrent?”

Mr Tudravu also acknowledged the value of CCTV footage in investigations but rejected suggestions Police only responded after videos appeared on social media.

He called for discussions on stronger deterrents and alternatives for people who had developed what he described as a worrying reliance on crime to earn a living.

“Crime prevention is everyone’s responsibility,” Mr Tudravu said.

item.title: Online safety laws under review
item.description: FIJI’s legal framework for dealing with cyber harm is being reviewed as the country responds to the growing challenges created by an increasingly digital society. Justice Minister and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga told Parliament on Wednesday last week that the Fiji Law Reform Commission was advancing its review of the Online Safety Act 2018.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’s legal framework for dealing with cyber harm is being reviewed as the country responds to the growing challenges created by an increasingly digital society.

Justice Minister and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga told Parliament on Wednesday last week that the Fiji Law Reform Commission was advancing its review of the Online Safety Act 2018.

The review has recently completed its final validation workshop, allowing stakeholders to provide feedback on an interim final report and draft Bill.

Mr Turaga said the review was aimed at strengthening Fiji’s legal response to harmful activity online.

“Its objective is very clear – to strengthen Fiji’s legal framework to better address cyber harm and challenges created by the increase in digital society,” he said.

“The final package is now being prepared for handover to my office this month.”

The review is one of several major law reform projects being undertaken by the commission, which also included the Mining Act 1965, Quarries Act, Security Industry Act 2010, Human Trafficking Laws and court rules.

Mr Turaga said the commission’s work reflected the need for laws to keep pace with technological and social change.

“Law reform is not simply about changing legislation for the sake of change – it is about asking more important questions.

“Are our laws still serving the people, the institutions and society they were created to serve?”

He said consultation remained a critical part of the process, with the people affected by legislation needing an opportunity to understand, question and contribute to its development.

“Good laws cannot be developed in isolation from the people who live under them.”

item.title: Hospital bed upgrade rolls out
item.description: Fiji’s health system is set for a major infrastructure boost, with the Ministry of Health rolling out 1502 new medical furniture and equipment units as part of a multi-year hospital bed upgrade program. Health and Medical Services Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu told Parliament that around 400 modern general hospital beds are expected to be delivered during the first phase of the program this financ
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s health system is set for a major infrastructure boost, with the Ministry of Health rolling out 1502 new medical furniture and equipment units as part of a multi-year hospital bed upgrade program.

Health and Medical Services Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu told Parliament that around 400 modern general hospital beds are expected to be delivered during the first phase of the program this financial year, targeting facilities facing the greatest pressure.

The Western Division will receive 84 beds for Nadi Hospital, 74 for Sigatoka Hospital, 43 for Rakiraki Hospital and 29 for Tavua Hospital. Labasa Hospital will receive specialised electric beds for its Coronary Care Unit and operating theatres, while Colonial War Memorial Hospital will receive new beds for several critical wards, including children’s, labour, postnatal, birthing and intensive care units.

Tamavua Twomey Hospital will also receive 39 beds for its Dermatology and Tuberculosis Ward.

The broader tender includes 779 general beds allocated across the divisions, along with specialised paediatric, psychiatric, cardiac and emergency beds, patient trolleys, electric examination couches, stretchers and wheelchairs.

Dr Lalabalavu said the three-year rollout would allow equipment to be properly inspected, installed and maintained while replacing ageing and unsafe equipment in facilities nationwide.

item.title: BE-GREEN to support 3050 rural households – Tunabuna
item.description: A NEW program is set to support thousands of rural households in Vanua Levu, with the Government promising stronger farming systems, healthier fishing grounds, ecosystem restoration and new economic opportunities. Minister for Agriculture and Waterways Tomasi Tunabuna told Parliament on Wednesday last week that the Blue Economy and Green Community Development Programme (BE-GREEN) was officially la
item.content:encoded:
A NEW program is set to support thousands of rural households in Vanua Levu, with the Government promising stronger farming systems, healthier fishing grounds, ecosystem restoration and new economic opportunities.

Minister for Agriculture and Waterways Tomasi Tunabuna told Parliament on Wednesday last week that the Blue Economy and Green Community Development Programme (BE-GREEN) was officially launched by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka on July 24 in Koronatoga Village, Cakaudrove.

“This landmark initiative reflects the Coalition Government’s unwavering commitment to safeguarding Fiji’s natural resources while creating sustainable economic opportunities for our rural communities,” Mr Tunabuna said.

The program, supported by the International Fund for Agricultural Development and the Global Environment Facility, will cover six Cakaudrove districts – Eastern Wailevu, Savusavu, Navatu, Koroalau, Vaturova and Naweni.

About 3050 subsistence and semi-commercial farming, fishing and handicraft-producing households are expected to benefit.

Mr Tunabuna said BE-GREEN would focus on boosting rural incomes, restoring ecosystems and strengthening communities against climate change and environmental degradation.

“The program has been designed to strengthen the productive capacity of Vanua Levu agriculture and marine sector through sustainable resource management, biodiversity enhancing practices, and climate smart approaches development.”

Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu backed the initiative but called for stronger implementation, monitoring and coordination.

He said women and youth participation were critical to tackling rural-urban migration.

“This is how we can create employment in the rural areas, and most importantly, empower them economically as well,” Mr Seruiratu said.

He also urged greater focus on agroforestry, reforestation, organic fertilisers and renewable energy.
